title: Historic Deal Positions FIA World Endurance Championship for Record Decade of Growth as the Sport Enters its Golden Age
summary: Sport news The Fédération Internationale de l'Automobile (FIA), the global governing body for motor sport and the federation for mobility organisations worldwide, and the Automobile Club de l’Ouest (ACO), the founder and organiser of the 24 Hours of Le Mans, have today announced a major deal for the FIA World Endurance Championship (FIA WEC), securing another decade of growth.   The landmark agreement, which comes during a period of unprecedented growth for the championship, will ensure a common ambition to expand the partnership and drive its commercial success. It will run from the end of 2027, when the current agreement expires, to the end of 2037.    Under the extended partnership agreement, all regulatory processes will be overseen by FIA Working Groups, the FIA Endurance Commission, and will require the final approval of the FIA World Motor Sport Council. The homologation process has also been streamlined, with the FIA and ACO overseeing the homologation of all cars competing in the Hypercar class.   The renewed partnership will also deliver significantly increased branding for the FIA. This includes enhanced branding prominently displayed across key areas including parc fermé, the podium and the Safety Cars, as well as across broadcast coverage.   With an expanding fanbase, a wider pool of competitors, and a global calendar of iconic events, the championship is stronger than ever. Since its inception in 2012, it has set the global standard for long-distance circuit racing. Following the introduction of the Hypercar regulations in 2021, interest in the championship from motor sport fans and from the automotive world has surged.    FIA WEC’s trackside audience has grown 8% so far in 2026, with millions of fans following the championship globally. The fanbase for the championship is also evolving. This year, 44% of attendees are aged 34 or younger, while 40% are attending an FIA WEC event for the first time. The championship has secured the long-term loyalty of its existing fanbase, while building the next generation of endurance racing fans.   Eight of the world’s leading auto-manufacturers currently compete in Hypercar, the top category of FIA WEC. Following the addition of the LMGT3 class in 2024, the championship now counts no fewer than 14 marques in total on the starting grid. Two more giants of the automotive industry – Ford and McLaren – are set to join the Hypercar ranks in 2027.   For over 100 years, endurance racing has served as a proven testbed for technologies that transfer from track to road. This renewed agreement creates a solid framework for advancing hydrogen powertrains in competition, providing a clear pathway toward more sustainable transport and mobility.    It will also deliver a more unified technical framework that defines top-level endurance racing Hypercars competing both in the FIA WEC and IMSA in North America, which will be introduced from 2030.  The new framework will provide greater cost-efficiency for manufacturers to compete in endurance racing championships and events globally, boosting potential participation and increasing the spectacle for motor sport fans.   With interest in FIA WEC at levels never seen before, the championship is positioned for continued growth and success over the coming decade. This new deal offers the solid foundation needed to secure its future, marking a milestone moment in the history of FIA WEC.    Mohammed Ben Sulayem, President of the FIA , said:  “This is not simply an agreement, it is a vital step forward for racing that will secure the future of the FIA World Endurance Championship for years to come.     “This is a deal built for the future, a deal of the century, one that strengthens the collaboration between the FIA and ACO, a relationship that dates back over 120 years, and sets the championship up for a decade of record growth that will deliver real benefits to fans, drivers, teams and manufacturers.     “It has been an honour to play a part in the collaboration that has helped usher in this golden age of endurance racing. I look forward to continuing our work alongside President Pierre Fillon and his team as we build on this momentum and shape an even stronger future.”     Pierre Fillon, President of the Automobile Club de l'Ouest , said: “ We are delighted to see the agreement between the FIA and the ACO extended, reinforcing the strong and long-standing relationship that has been at the heart of the FIA World Endurance Championship since its creation in 2012. This partnership has been built on trust, shared ambition, and a common commitment to the development of endurance racing.      “Together, the FIA and the ACO have created a solid foundation for the continued success and international growth of the championship, and we look forward to writing the next chapter of this remarkable collaboration. Finally, I would like to thank FIA President Mohammed Ben Sulayem for the great relationship we have built.”      Alberto Villarreal, General Manager at the FIA , said:  “The FIA World Endurance Championship is stronger and more popular than it has ever been before, with a growing and evolving fanbase, and an impressive roster of top-tier global auto-manufacturers.      “The agreement announced today underlines the investment in the championship from both the FIA and the ACO, and our commitment to continue bringing the sport to new audiences. It is a pivotal moment in the history of FIA WEC, and provides the foundation and stability needed for the championship’s ongoing success.”      Frédéric Lequien, CEO of the Le Mans Endurance Management, the promoter for the FIA World Endurance Championship , said:  “This agreement comes at an exciting time for the FIA World Endurance Championship. The championship is experiencing exceptional momentum, with growing engagement from manufacturers, teams, partners, media, and fans around the world. The extension provides a strong framework to build on this growth, further strengthen the global appeal of the WEC and continue to deliver a world-class championship at the forefront of endurance racing. We are looking forward to an ambitious and exciting future for the FIA WEC.”     -   Notes to Editors     The renewed agreement between the FIA and the ACO follows three other significant long-term agreement announcements since July 2025:      FIA and Formula E sign landmark extension to power Formula E World Championship for another 10 years, announced in July 2025 –  information here        Multi-year Concorde Governance Agreement between the FIA, Formula 1 Group and all 11 race teams, announced in December 2025 –  information here        “Deal of the Century” for FIA World and European Rally Championships in July 2026 –  information here         These announcements form part of the FIA’s strategic investment in the future of motor sport, as it continues its mission to grow participation in the sport and provide a safe and accessible platform for all.      The FIA has seen a radical transformation since 2021, and earlier this year  announced  that it had delivered its strongest set of financial results in a decade in 2025, with an operating profit of €6.7m. It also reported an exceptional gain of €20m through the Formula E contract extension.    About the FIA  The Fédération Internationale de l'Automobile (FIA) is the governing body for world motor sport and the federation for mobility organisations globally. It is a non-profit organisation committed to driving innovation and championing safety, sustainability and equality across motor sport and mobility.   Founded in 1904, with offices in Paris, London and Geneva, the FIA brings together 246 Member Organisations across five continents, representing millions of road users, motor sport professionals and volunteers. It develops and enforces regulations for motor sport, including six FIA World Championships, to ensure worldwide competitions are safe and fair for all.    About the ACO   Founded in 1906, the Automobile Club de l’Ouest (ACO) is the creator and organiser of major motorsport events: the first Grand Prix in history in 1906, followed by the 24 Hours of Le Mans starting in 1923. The ACO has also been the organiser and promoter of the FIA World Endurance Championship (FIA WEC) since 2012 and the creator of continental series: the European Le Mans Series (2004) and the Asian Le Mans Series (2013). The ACO organises the 24 Hours of Le Mans Motorcycle Race, the 24 Hours of Le Mans Karting, the 24 Hours of Le Mans Truck Race, and the French Motorcycle Grand Prix on its Le Mans circuits…   The 24 Hours of Le Mans serves as a true technological laboratory focused on automotive innovation. It is in this spirit that the ACO continues to evolve. Sustainable mobility - embodied in particular by MissionH24, which aims to introduce hydrogen to the 24 Hours of Le Mans - is a key objective for the ACO.   Since 2024, the ACO has held the FIA’s 3-star environmental accreditation and is ISO 20121 certified, the benchmark for responsible event management. In September 2024, the 24 Hours of Le Mans circuit was also voted “France’s Favourite Monument.”    About FIA WEC  The FIA World Endurance Championship (FIA WEC), created in 2012 by the Fédération Internationale de l’Automobile (FIA) and the Automobile Club de l’Ouest (ACO), represents the undisputed pinnacle of the long-distance discipline.   Bringing together the world’s leading manufacturers, biggest brands, top drivers and most successful teams, FIA WEC races around the globe, pushing the limits of speed, performance and durability while encouraging ever-greater feats of strategic skill. If the fast and fearless drivers are the heroes, then the cars are the stars, from their cutting-edge technology to their dynamic design. And then, of course, there is the sound of the engines – that uncompromising, unadulterated roar.   The cornerstone of the calendar is the iconic 24 Hours of Le Mans, an event born in 1923 that continues to serve as the ultimate test for manufacturers seeking to prove their mettle – but every race has its own character, challenges and pitfalls. As a series with a proud history, a compelling present and a thrilling future, FIA WEC remains endurance racing’s global benchmark, continuously setting the standard in the sport and inspiring generations to come. title: FIA Asia Pacific Congress to Bring Member Clubs Together in the Philippines to Advance Mobility and Motor Sport Across the Region
summary: Members news    The Fédération Internationale de l'Automobile (FIA), the global governing body for motor sport and the federation for mobility organisations worldwide, will be hosted by the Automobile Association Philippines (AAP) in Boracay in the Philippines for its Asia Pacific Congress next week, bringing together FIA Member Clubs from across the region.  From 29 September to 1 October, 120 delegates from Member Clubs across Asia and the Pacific, will unite in Boracay for three days of collaboration, innovation and knowledge sharing. Throughout the week, attendees will discuss priorities to advance safe and sustainable mobility for road users and drive greater motor sport accessibility.  The Asia-Pacific region is one of the FIA's most diverse and dynamic, spanning some of the world's fastest-growing mobility markets and an expanding motor sport community. The Congress will provide Member Clubs with an opportunity to share expertise and develop practical solutions which respond to the specific needs of their members and communities.  Across mobility, discussions will focus on road safety, innovation, sustainable and accessible transport, tourism and the changing needs of road users, building on the FIA's work to support Clubs in delivering meaningful impact at a national and regional level.  Motor sport sessions will explore opportunities to increase participation, strengthen grassroots competition and create more accessible pathways into the sport, supporting the FIA's ambition to make motor sport more affordable and accessible around the world.  The programme will also showcase the work and innovation of FIA Member Clubs across Asia-Pacific, providing a platform to share successful initiatives which can be adapted and scaled across the region.   H.E. Mohammed Ben Sulayem, President of the FIA, said:   "The Asia-Pacific region is central to the future of both mobility and motor sport, and our Member Clubs are at the heart of that progress.   From improving road safety and embracing innovation to creating new opportunities for people to participate in motor sport, our Clubs are delivering real impact for their communities.    "The FIA Asia Pacific Congress gives us an important opportunity to bring that expertise together, share ideas and strengthen collaboration across one of the most diverse and dynamic regions in our Federation.    "I thank our hosts the Automobile Association Philippines, and President Joe Ferreria, for welcoming the FIA family to Boracay and look forward to another productive Congress."    FIA Region II President and President of host club the Automobile Association Philippines, Augustus ‘Joe’ Ferreria said:   "The strength of this region comes from the diversity, knowledge and ambition of our Member Clubs. Bringing our community together in the Philippines gives us the opportunity to learn from one another, identify shared challenges and develop solutions that can support Clubs across the region.    "The Asia Pacific Congress is an important moment for us to build on the progress already being made and ensure our Clubs have the tools, knowledge and connections they need to continue growing.    "We are proud to welcome the FIA and our fellow Member Clubs from across Asia-Pacific to the Philippines.”   The Congress follows a period of significant activity for the FIA across the region.  The FIA has expanded its  Safe Mobility 4 All & 4 Life  programme into Asia-Pacific, supporting Member Clubs and authorities with training and practical tools to improve road safety, while initiatives including the  FIA Innovation Challenge  continue to showcase Club-led solutions which can be shared and scaled across the Federation.  Across motor sport, the region continues to play an important role at every level of competition, from grassroots participation and regional championships through to the FIA's major World Championships with Malaysia set to host the Bahrain Grand Prix in the days following the congress.  The FIA Member Club structure forms the backbone of the federation’s governance and operations, with each full Member Club holding voting rights across the FIA’s elections and regulatory decisions. Clubs are grouped into two primary categories, with some serving in both roles:   Mobility Clubs – provide mobility services and represent the interest of road users, with a focus on road safety, travel and tourism, consumer rights, and sustainable mobility  National Sporting Authorities (ASNs) – govern and develop motorsport at a national level, are responsible for sporting events, issuing licenses, and engagement across regulations   Within the FIA there are four Mobility Regions and 6 sport zones. The FIA Asia Pacific Congress will welcome Member Clubs from across the region. The global FIA Membership is comprised of 246 clubs across five continents, connecting over 80 million members.      -ENDS-      For media enquiries please contact:   Geri Sherwin, Director of Presidential and Mobility Communications:  gsherwin@fia.com   George Mitchell, Mobility Communications Officer:  gmitchell@fia.com        About the Fédération Internationale de l'Automobile    The Fédération Internationale de l'Automobile (FIA) is the governing body for world motor sport and the federation for mobility organisations globally. title: ‘DEAL OF THE CENTURY’ PAYING DIVIDENDS FOR FIA WORLD RALLY CHAMPIONSHIP AS FORD RACING CONFIRMS ITS RETURN FROM 2028
summary: Sport news The Fédération Internationale de l’Automobile (FIA), the global governing body for motor sport and the federation for mobility organisations worldwide, has today welcomed Ford’s announcement that it will return to the FIA World Rally Championship with a full factory programme from 2028 and develop an all-new Rally1 car under the FIA’s WRC27 technical regulations for 2029.  Ford’s return to the championship will mark its first full works programme in the FIA WRC since 2012 and comes at a significant moment in the championship’s development. With new technical regulations arriving in 2027, increased investment under new ownership and plans to expand the WRC’s presence in key markets including the United Kingdom and United States, the series is entering a new period of sporting and commercial growth.  The announcement makes Ford the fourth constructor to commit to developing a car under the FIA’s new WRC27 technical regulations. Designed around safety, affordability, flexibility and accessibility, the regulations will reduce the cost of competing at the highest level of rallying, with the price of a ready-to-compete car capped at €345,000 in asphalt specification.  From 2028, Ford Racing will become directly involved in its FIA WRC programme alongside long-standing partner M-Sport, before introducing an all-new Rally1 car developed to the WRC27 technical regulations in 2029. The commitment reflects the growing attractiveness of the FIA World Rally Championship to global automotive manufacturers and reinforces the role of FIA World Championships as genuine laboratories for the development, testing and demonstration of future technologies.  Ford’s commitment follows growing interest in the new regulations from both global automotive manufacturers and independent constructors and comes as the championship has recently secured the ‘Deal of the Century’ and enters a new period of commercial development under its recently appointed promoter team.  The growing manufacturer interest also underlines the wider role of the FIA’s World Championships as global platforms for automotive manufacturers to develop and demonstrate new technologies, test solutions in demanding competition environments and transfer knowledge between motor sport and road-going vehicles.  Ford’s return to the WRC also forms part of an expanding global motor sport programme. The Blue Oval returned to the FIA Formula One World Championship in 2026, competes in the FIA World Rally-Raid Championship and is preparing to return to the top category of the FIA World Endurance Championship in 2027, having already launched its LMGT3 programme. Its WRC programme will give Ford a presence across four FIA World Championships from 2028.  Ford has played a major role in the history of the FIA World Rally Championship, with cars including the Escort, Sierra, Focus, Fiesta and Puma competing across more than five decades of international rallying.   FIA President Mohammed Ben Sulayem, said : “Today’s announcement represents another significant moment for the FIA World Rally Championship. With a new promoter in place, three constructors already committed to the new technical regulations, and now Ford confirming its return as a full works manufacturer, there is real momentum behind the championship’s next era.  “Ford is one of the great names in motorsport and its commitment to FIA World Championships continues to grow. The manufacturer returned to Formula 1 this year, is competing at the highest level of the FIA World Rally-Raid Championship, will return to the top category of the FIA World Endurance Championship in 2027, and from 2028 will once again compete as a works manufacturer in the WRC. That will give Ford a presence across four FIA World Championships and demonstrates the importance it places on motor sport as a global platform, and laboratory, for its brand, products and technologies.  “I had the privilege of driving for Ford during my own career, so welcoming them back is a particularly special moment for me. The WRC continues to grow, and this long-term commitment from such an iconic manufacturer is a testament to the strength of the championship.”   Jim Baumbick, President of Ford Europe, said:  “Rallying is where Ford’s character faces its toughest test, and where generations of fans come to share the thrill of seeing a car take on the impossible. We want our next generation of European vehicles to carry that same unapologetic spirit. Responsive, confidence-inspiring, and rewarding to drive on the roads people use every day.”   Mark Rushbrook, Global Director, Ford Racing, said:  “As we celebrate 125 years of Ford Racing, our 50-year legacy in the WRC stands out as one of our proudest because of its direct connection to the fun and exciting cars that came from that. We can’t wait to compete again in rally racing in 2028 and beyond.”   Eric Boullier, CEO of WRC Promoter, said: “ Ford’s decision to return to the FIA World Rally Championship as a full factory team is fantastic news. The brand has an extraordinary history in rallying and has been part of some of the sport’s most memorable moments. More importantly, this renewed commitment to WRC, as part of its extensive global motorsport programme, is a strong statement about the relevance of rallying to one of the world’s leading automotive brands.  “Seeing WRC support both its racing ambitions and the development of future road cars is particularly exciting. We are delighted to welcome Ford back as a full factory team and look forward to this new chapter together.”   Notes to editors:    WRC27 Constructors   Prior to the announcement that Ford will return to the FIA World Rally Championship and develop a new-generation Rally1 car under the WRC27 regulations, three Constructors had already committed to developing cars for the championship’s next technical era:   Toyota has committed to developing a new-generation Rally1 car under the WRC27 regulations.  Project Rally One is developing a new WRC27 car as an independent Constructor project.  WRT Rally1 Spain is developing a new WRC27 Rally1 car as a further independent Constructor project.   Ford’s announcement makes it the fourth Constructor to commit to developing a car under the WRC27 technical regulations.  The WRC27 regulations will come into effect from 2027 and allow both OEMs (Manufacturers) and independent projects to design, homologate and compete with cars at the highest level of the FIA World Rally Championship.  The regulations have been developed to reduce costs, broaden participation and provide long-term stability for the championship. A ready-to-compete WRC27 car in asphalt specification will be capped at  €345,000  ,  significantly lowering the cost of competing at the highest level of world rallying. It is a non-profit organisation committed to driving innovation and championing safety, sustainability and equality across motor sport and mobility.  Founded in 1904, with offices in Paris, London and Geneva, the FIA brings together 246 Member Organisations across five continents, representing millions of road users, motor sport professionals and volunteers. It develops and enforces regulations for motor sport, including six FIA World Championships, to ensure worldwide competitions are safe and fair for all. PG:  Yeah, it's all fine. I mean, you know, in the heat of the moment you're running high on adrenaline, you're running high on emotion, frustration, disappointment, race over. And yeah, it was a big blow for us as a team, but the only way of going forward is just to get back together and get stronger as a team. And, you know, we all need each other to finish in the fifth place this year, and we'll need each other next year. And we've got to look ahead. And, you know, he came to apologise. It was an unfortunate mistake that, you know, once you pass that line and you brake too late, out of control, and it was just unfortunate that I was the car that he shunted into. Yeah, it's done. Slept over it a couple of days and now in Malaysia and looking forward.    Q: (Ronald Vording – Motorsport.com) Another one to Pierre, but this time a different topic. We haven't had a proper wet session this season yet, both when it comes to the tyres that drivers complain about a lot, but also the '26 cars and some of the measures that the FIA has taken, are you confident that everything is in good shape if it ends up wet here?   PG:  I think out of any track in the season, if one is good for wet, it's probably here. So, you know, you'll ask me about Vegas in crazy cold conditions and, well, still could happen there. It was probably going to be definitely more tricky. But here the track's really rough, it's really hot, there's a bit of elevation, so it should be pretty good to clear the track in terms of water quantity. So I think it will be fine. But I think the only time I tried was, you know, in January in Silverstone, which was horrendous, and then in Magny-Cours with extremely cold conditions, which didn't feel good at all. But I expect it to be in a much better place here.    Q: (Adam Cooper – Adam Cooper F1) For Lance and Pierre, you both know Esteban really well. Are you a bit disappointed to see him without a drive for next year, and how good is he at this stage in his career? Lance, you can take that first.   Lance STROLL:  Yeah, I mean, Formula 1's not always fair and, you know, sometimes you're in situations where it's just s**t. And, you know, that's kind of, I think, the situation he's in. I think he's demonstrated over the years that, you know, he's been great in Formula 1 and he's had a lot of good results. So, you know, it definitely sucks for him. And all I can say is I really hope he bounces back and he finds himself in a good situation in the near future. If that's here, if that's somewhere else, if that's, you know, whatever. I just, you know, only wish him the best. You know, he's a great driver and, like I said, he's demonstrated that in Formula 1, not just in Formula 1 but all of his junior years. I was racing in Prema in a similar time to him in our junior career, and I was in F4 and he was in F3, and, you know, he was winning all those races and stuff. And even when we were in karting together, he was always really quick. And yeah, so I only wish him the best.     Q: Pierre, your thoughts?   PG:  Yeah, I mean, I can only agree with Lance. It's a tricky situation, to say the least, and I think at the end of the day it should not take away the almost 200 starts he's had in Formula 1. So I don't think many drivers have achieved that in their career, and it is still something to be very proud of. And in terms of performance, you know, at the end of the day the results speak for themselves. He didn't have the easiest of seasons this year, but it’s not all down to him. And yeah, he's achieved a lot in his time in F1.    Q: (Adam Cooper – Adam Cooper F1) For all three of you, several of your colleagues have just had a boys' holiday together on an island. Were any of you invited, or is the idea of a few days with a bunch of racing drivers a bit of a nightmare? Arvid, you take that one first.   AL:  I didn't get the invite, but honestly, my dream few days off is not with other drivers.    Q: Lance, same?   LS:  Same, yeah.    Q: Did you get the invite and would you have gone?   LS:  No.    Q: (  Qui Chao – Tencent Sports) I have questions for all three drivers. Sepang is a very comprehensive track with two long straights and several straight-line modes. Based on simulator runs, how demanding is this track on energy management, and does this layout favour overtaking with this generation of cars? Arvid, would you like to start?   AL:  Yeah, I don't remember the first part of the question. I don't think it'll be too bad with energy. I mean, none of us have driven here for a while, so I don't think we really know, but I don't think it'll be too bad. I think it will be a more normal experience. And then overtaking difficulty, I think, will actually be on the easier side. And I also think the boost will be relatively powerful on this track because of the layout. So I think, yeah, we'll go towards good racing and lots of overtaking opportunities.    Q: Pierre, your thoughts?   PG:  Yeah, same. Should be good for overtakes and energy, to be fair, I can't really... Yeah, I'll see tomorrow.    Q: Lance, anything to add?   LS:  No.    Q: (Ronald Vording – Motorsport.com) It's one for Pierre, but the others can add if they want to. Fernando said a couple of times in recent weeks that he still has hopes for more regulation changes going into next year. He proposed something in Baku to get some more natural speed traces again and reach a top speed towards the braking zones. Do you think that more is needed, or are you happy to first try what's in place for '27 now?   PG:  I mean, I'm not fully aware of all the changes. I know some of them, which are definitely heading in the right direction. I think overall we've just got to find a way to fine-tune with the tools we have. And I think we all agree we need to make it better. I don't think anyone's fully satisfied with what we've got at the minute. And, I mean, we have a couple of months before starting 2027, and I think anything that can be done with what we've got at the minute needs to be done to improve drivability and improve racing. We're going to enjoy it more at the wheel and I'm sure people will enjoy it as well more from the outside.    Q: Are you giving constant feedback?   PG:  I think, to be fair, with the FIA and F1 it's been a very good relationship in terms of being honest with what we have now. We have a common goal of making F1 better for everyone and they've received our feedback very well, whether it's good or bad. I think we're always very straight with them, for the only goal of making our sport better.    Q: (Adam Cooper – Adam Cooper F1) For all three of you, what are your thoughts on potentially racing at Imola in December? Obviously, a couple of you know Faenza, you know the area pretty well, you've tested there in the winter in terms of the weather, the daylight hours and so on. Arvid, would you like to take that first?   AL:  It'll be a bit colder than Abu Dhabi. Yeah, I don't know. I think, I mean, in the end we'll do whatever F1 think is best. I know they're managing it. I don't know all the ins and outs of what's happening, but I've heard that Imola is the backup. So yeah, let's see. I think, I mean, yes, it will get a bit darker a bit earlier, but I think there's still enough hours for us to drive fine, so I don't think that would be an issue. It'll just be a bit cold, maybe wet.    Q: Lance, any thoughts on racing in Imola in December?   LS:  I like Imola.    Q: Pierre?   PG:  I love Imola.    Q: And it's closer to your home, I guess?   PG:  Well, I mean, it's another Italian Grand Prix. Yeah, I mean, we'll see. I'm sure we're going to find a way to make it work. It's just going to be cold if eventually we go there. title: A Lifesaving Call, a Mobility Lifeline, and a Solar-Powered Guardian | Region II Champions Announced for FIA Innovation Challenge 2026
summary: Mobility news The Fédération Internationale de l'Automobile (FIA), the global governing body for motor sport and the federation for mobility organisations worldwide, has revealed the Region II (Asia-Pacific) Champions of the FIA Innovation Challenge 2026, celebrating the projects that are driving mobility solutions across the Asia-Pacific Region.   Announced as Region II Champions at the FIA Asia-Pacific Congress in Boracay, Philippines, were FIA Member Clubs:     Royal Automobile Club of Victoria (RACV, Australia; Member of the Australian Automobile Association) for ‘ Asure eCall ’, an integrated technology which automatically triggers an emergency call after a crash.       Automobile Association of Ceylon (AAC, Sri Lanka) for ‘ AAC Mobility Lifeline ’, which transformed it’s 24-hour call centre into a national mobility coordination hub in response to Cyclone Ditwah.       AAC received a second award for its ‘ Solar-Guard ’ LED blinker system, giving drivers advanced warning about potential hazards at high-risk locations.     Now in its third year, the FIA Innovation Challenge has seen Member Clubs throughout Region II reinforcing their commitment to supporting individuals and businesses with solutions for safer, more sustainable, and more affordable mobility.    Intelematics and its parent organisation, the RACV, are leveraging the technology of connected vehicles to trigger rapid emergency calls and responses in the event of a crash, while the AAC has showcased how working with its mobility partners supported national resilience and recovery following Cyclone Ditwah. The AAC is also proactively preventing crashes with a solar-powered early-warning system.   H.E. Mohammed Ben Sulayem, President of the FIA said: “ Congratulations to all our Region II Champions and thank you to every Member Club who has continued innovating for road users across the Asia-Pacific Region.     “The projects submitted this year have highlighted the real difference our Clubs can make in times of crisis and how constant innovation is helping us to reduce the risk of crashes and save lives on the road.”    Tim Shearman, FIA Deputy President for Automobile Mobility and Tourism said:  “We are a global network, but it’s the local knowledge of our Mobility Clubs that helps us meet the unique needs of road users everywhere.      “Innovation in mobility is how we improve the lives of road users, and our Region II Champions have embodied that spirit and showcased new solutions that can make a difference locally and across the FIA Network.”    Augustus ‘Joe’ Ferreria, FIA Region II President said:  “Mobility in FIA Region II is diverse and unique and complex, and so are our challenges, so our Mobility Clubs have to work hard to ensure they are always there for the road users they support.     “Our Region has seen the devastating consequences of extreme weather and dangerous roads, and I am so proud to see how these projects have put our Mobility Clubs at the heart of the solution for everyone on the road.”    The FIA Innovation Challenge is an annual contest promoting and celebrating impactful and scalable business and services projects from Member Clubs in the four global Mobility Regions across the FIA Network (Asia Pacific / Europe, Middle East and Africa / North America / South and Central America).    Three champions will be selected from each of the four Mobility Regions, with a global judging panel selecting one Global Winner from each Region, who will receive their awards at the FIA General Assemblies week in Shanghai, China, in December.    The Winning Submissions:    Before the Sirens | Reimagining Connected Crash Response ( RACV, Australia )    Roads in Australia present unique challenges where crashes may occur in remote locations, dangerous environments, and may be hours from the nearest ambulance. Intelematics and its parent organisation, the RACV, have developed the ‘Asure’ connected vehicle platform to trigger an immediate response from connected vehicles when a crash occurs, even if the occupants are unconscious. By automatically transmitting a call with critical data to trained call centre staff, Asure allows for rapid assessment and engagement with emergency services. Intelematics has now expanded Asure into the New Zealand market and supports over 1 million vehicles.   Rob Finney, General Manager, Intelematics said:  “Being involved in a crash is one of the most frightening and dangerous situations a person can experience. Add to that being potentially hundreds of kilometres away from help and unable to make a call, and you have a scary scenario that unfortunately some road users have faced on our regional roads.      “We built Asure so the call for help starts the moment a crash happens, not when someone happens to drive past. Our agents have the crash data within seconds and get it to emergency services quickly and accurately, so help can be on its way sooner. Being recognised by the FIA is a proud moment for our team and the partners who helped shape this platform.”     AAC Mobility Lifeline | Beyond the Call of Duty ( AAC, Sri Lanka )    Cyclone Ditwah struck Sri Lanka in November 2025, causing major disruption for mobility across the country. In response, the AAC activated ‘AAC Mobility’, transforming its 24-hour call centre into a national mobility coordination hub. With a 200% increase in emergency calls, the AAC guided road users, rescue services and evacuees through flooded roads and landslides to safety. Alongside 60 staff, over 135 volunteers, and 50 vehicles, the AAC also mobilised its network of more than 160 accredited garages, demonstrating the importance of local partnerships to support nationwide resilience and recovery during a crisis. As part of its ongoing efforts, AAC has contributed Rs. 25 million to the President’s Fund to support the Government Policy on “Clean Sri Lanka” towards those affected by Cyclone Ditwah.   Dhammika Attygalle, President of the AAC said:  “Extreme weather events are becoming more common, creating uncertainty and increasing risks for road users. So having a network ready to respond when they need us most is vital.     “Cyclone Ditwah showcased the vulnerability of our roads to extreme weather but also demonstrated the power of our partnerships in Sri Lanka. Our people and our community are the driving force behind AAC Mobility Lifeline and our road to recovery.”      Solar-Guard Road Safety Blinking System | Flash to Stop the Crash ( AAC, Sri Lanka )    Sharp bends and hilly terrain coupled with limited visibility and delayed reaction time make Sri Lanka’s highways the site of frequent crashes. To proactively reduce these risks, the AAC, in collaboration with the Road Development Authority, created a solar-powered advanced-warning system, introducing LED blinker lights to high-risk areas. With 24-hour, autonomous visual alerts improving driver awareness, the ‘Solar-Guard’ system is reducing crashes while operating sustainably without dependence on the grid.   Dhammika Attygalle, President of the AAC said:  “Limited visibility on hazardous roads puts drivers at increased risk of being involved in a crash, so finding ways to proactively prevent these incidents from occurring in the first place is essential for protecting road users.     “Through this solar-powered system, we have implemented a sustainable solution to increase visibility for road users in hazardous areas at all times to reduce crashes and save lives.”           -ENDS-        For media enquiries please contact:      George Mitchell, Mobility Communications Officer:  gmitchell@fia.com         Laure Mercier Roussel, Head of Mobility Communications:  lmercier@fia.com        About the Fédération Internationale de l'Automobile       The Fédération Internationale de l'Automobile (FIA) is the governing body for world motor sport and the federation for mobility organisations globally. It is a non-profit organisation committed to driving innovation and championing safety, sustainability and equality across motor sport and mobility.      Founded in 1904, with offices in Paris, London and Geneva, the FIA brings together 246 Member Organisations across five continents, representing millions of road users, motor sport professionals and volunteers. It develops and enforces regulations for motor sport, including six FIA World Championships, to ensure worldwide competitions are safe and fair for all.      FIA INNOVATION CHALLENGE  FIA  Members  Region II   Mobility 1MobilityFIA INNOVATION CHALLENGEFIAMembersRegion II00 Thursday, October 1, 2026 - 6:50am  Thursday, October 1, 2026 - 6:50am

title: Goodyear FIA ETRC Le Mans raceday two round-up: Champion Kiss doubles up in style as Smith shines
summary: Sport news Despite wrapping up the coveted crown in yesterday’s opening race, Kiss continued his pursuit of Goodyear FIA ETRC glory during the final day of the 24 Heures Camions weekend at the famous French venue.  He set a stunning lap of 2m03.820s around the 4.185-kilometre Circuit Bugatti in second qualifying this morning to bank pole position number 12 of 2026. His qualifying best in 2025 was a 2m04.322s.  The MAN-powered Révész Racing driver then secured the Race 3 win by a commanding margin of 8.801s ahead of six-time champion Jochen Hahn with Sascha Lenz finishing third to continue his push for the runner-up spot in the final title standings behind Kiss.  But the Hungarian hero left his best to last when he charged through from eighth on the Race 4 reverse grid to win ahead of Chrome star Bradley Smith – who led overall for four laps – and Antonio Albacete.     Points scored by Kiss and René Reinert at Le Mans ensured their Révész-Reinert Racing Team won the Goodyear FIA European Truck Racing Championship for Teams* with one round remaining.  Having snatched the Goodyear FIA ETRC Chrome points lead from defending champion Mark Taylor by winning the category in Race 2 yesterday, John Newell edged ahead of his British rival with a second consecutive victory in Race 3 before Smith took the honours in Race 4 having also triumphed in Race 1. Newell finished second with Taylor in third. Heading into the Jarama season showdown next weekend (3-4 October), Newell leads Taylor by 13 points.  After winning Race 2 on Saturday, José Eduardo Rodrigues’ Le Mans weekend got even better when he wrapped up the Goodyear FIA ETRC Young Driver crown* in Race 3. However, the third-generation competitor from Portugal suffered a frustrating Race 4 when he ran wide and dropped back while running in second place. He recovered to 10th place from 14th. Then he gave me back the position, so I guess he felt the same. From there I just had the pace, did my race, push away and built a gap. It was a good race, nice conditions but the Goodyear tyres held up very well. The start was a bit strange but other than that it worked out very well. For sure it was hotter conditions than yesterday, but we had good pace and I’m very proud of the team, Révész Racing, a big thank you to them.”   Race 3 Chrome winner John Newell said:  “Bradley [Smith] had a few good nibbles at me in the first lap or so, but we got set up a bit aggressive from qualifying and burned my front tyre in the first three laps and hit two penalty markers, so for the rest of the race I had to back it down and be so careful. Steffi [Halm] was on Bradley’s back all the time, so I knew I’d pull a gap. I just kept my head down and make sure I didn’t hit a penalty marker, take full points and that’s me good. We left the same set-up [after qualifying] and we should have made it a bit less aggressive, but we didn’t know how it was going to be because it’s a completely new set-up, but now we can alter it for Race 4.”   Race 4 winner Norbert Kiss said:  “For sure I had a good start and could overtake Jochen [Hahn] after the first chicane. In front of me there was a bit of chaos and there was some luck included with people making mistakes so those were some easy overtakes. But I had some more difficult ones, like on René [Reinert] on the braking zone at the first chicane or against John Newell on the outside of Turn 4 I think, so I made some good moves. Overall, I’m happy because it’s very difficult to win the reverse-grid race and I happy it worked out this way. We also closed the Teams’ championship together with René, so very happy to win the Teams’ championship as well because the guys from Révész Racing and Reinert Racing worked really hard. We go to Jarama [for the final round now]. Of course all the pressure is off, but we don’t lay back, we keep pushing because you’re only worth as much as your last race. Jarama is a circuit I love, it’s been very good for us in the past with some very nice and very important victories there. We try to do the maximum as well and enjoy maximum the weekend and enjoy the success of the season.”   Race 4 Chrome winner Bradley Smith said:  “I don’t think I breathed for the last 15 minutes. I was really nervous at the start, but I managed to get a good start and get into the lead. I made a few silly mistakes, there was a bit of over-driving and then I see the red bullet (Kiss) behind me. I managed to keep him behind me for a few laps but then I locked up around the back. I’m happy for the team, it’s my first overall podium and do it at Le Mans seems special with the Chrome win as well. I don’t think I could have held Norbi off for that long, but I take [the result] all day long, keeping improving and improving.”    All drivers race with Goodyear’s new-for-2026 tyre, which features 60 per cent sustainable materials. title: FIA President Mohammed Ben Sulayem meets with Azerbaijani President Ilham Aliyev as Baku Celebrates a Decade of Racing
summary: FIA news His Excellency Mohammed Ben Sulayem, President of the Fédération Internationale de l'Automobile (FIA), met with His Excellency Ilham Aliyev, President of the Republic of Azerbaijan, in Baku today to discuss shared priorities across motorsport and mobility.  The meeting, which took place during the Baku Grand Prix as the city celebrated a decade of racing on its iconic streets, provided an opportunity to discuss Azerbaijan’s continued development as a major international sporting destination, its established position within global motorsport, and opportunities to strengthen cooperation between the country and the FIA.  Azerbaijan has become an important destination on the international sporting calendar, with Baku providing one of Formula 1’s most distinctive city-centre settings and attracting fans and visitors from around the world.  The Presidents also discussed the wider role of mobility in supporting economic growth and connectivity, as well as the importance of road safety and sustainable transport as Azerbaijan continues to invest in its infrastructure and international connectivity.   FIA President, H.E. Mohammed Ben Sulayem said:   “It was a pleasure to meet with His Excellency President Ilham Aliyev and discuss our shared ambitions for the continued development of motorsport and mobility in Azerbaijan.    “The success of Formula 1 in Baku demonstrates what can be achieved through long-term commitment, strong organisation and a clear vision for the role that major sporting events can play in bringing people together and showcasing a country to the world. My congratulations on a fantastic ten years of racing and I look forward to many more.    “Our discussions also extended beyond motorsport. As the global federation for mobility organisations, the FIA is committed to working with governments and our Member Clubs such as the Azerbaijan Automobile Federation to make mobility safer, more accessible and more sustainable. I look forward to continuing our collaboration with our partners in Azerbaijan across these important areas.”   President Ben Sulayem’s visit comes as the FIA continues to strengthen its engagement across the region through its global network of Member Clubs and partners, including the Azerbaijan Automobile Federation and its President Anar Alakbarov.  The FIA has placed significant emphasis on growing motorsport participation and strengthening the pathway from grassroots competition to the highest levels of the sport, while using its global mobility network to advance road safety, sustainable mobility and accessibility. Azerbaijan’s position at the crossroads of Europe and Asia, alongside continued investment in transport and infrastructure, provides opportunities for further collaboration across both pillars of the FIA’s work.  The meeting formed part of President Ben Sulayem’s programme in Azerbaijan, bringing together government, motorsport and mobility stakeholders to discuss opportunities to further develop the FIA’s activities in the country and wider region.        ENDS    About the FIA   The Fédération Internationale de l'Automobile (FIA) is the governing body for world motor sport and the federation for mobility organisations globally. title: F1 - 2026 Azerbaijan Grand Prix Post-Race Press Conference Transcript
summary: Sport news  DRIVERS    1 – George RUSSELL (Mercedes)   2 – Max VERSTAPPEN (Red Bull Racing)   3 – Isack HADJAR (Red Bull Racing)       TRACK INTERVIEWS     (Conducted by Timo Glock)        Q: George, we see that big smile back on your face. That tells it all. I mean, it looked like an easy Saturday drive through Baku, but it got really spicy at the end. Talk us through those last laps.    George RUSSELL:  Yeah, I mean, it was amazing to be back on the top step of the podium. So, I do want to say a big thanks to my team because, you know, they’ve continued to believe in me through a tough moment, helped me come through it. I’m really proud to have had this weekend. And then, yeah, the first half of the race felt pretty plain sailing, getting a gap. Safety Car restart, especially when I saw Max behind, I thought, you know, it’s not going to be easy. And he drove incredibly at the end of the race. And then when the yellow flag came out, I lifted off the power and when I went back, I had no turbo, so then I had no power. Max almost got me at the line. So, yeah, that would have been a real shame. But all in all, incredible weekend.      Q: But what is it? I mean, it looked like you came in this weekend, from lap one on, you had this confidence back. What changed in getting that performance out of the car?    GR:  I think it’s just having more experience with this sort of new driving style I’ve adopted. And every race since the break, I feel like I’ve gone from strength to strength and I feel like more myself again. So that’s really great.      Q: Well, Max, what a drive again, from P8 to P2, you came less than two tenths short, but how satisfying is that, to be back on the podium and having the chance of putting George under pressure?    Max VERSTAPPEN:  Yeah, we had a good race. I mean, the first stint was probably a little bit difficult with the Medium tyre, but we still worked our way into P3 and then we had a good restart, into P2. Then it was just like, 1 second, 1.1s. Then on the final lap, with the yellow flag, I think, George lost a bit of boost out of one corner and that’s why I caught up quite a bit and then to the line, I got close, but it was not enough.      Q: But Max, you threw everything at it. I mean, you brushed the walls a couple of times. I mean, that last wall, was that a sketchy one or was it sort of still under control?    MV:  It was okay. I just tried to open the corner probably a little bit too much, but the tyres were fine.      Q: Isack, I mean, what a comeback. Six weeks off, being on the podium. I mean, how happy are you coming back with a podium and a double podium for Red Bull?    Isack HADJAR:  Yeah, I’m happy. You know, it’s been very long, six weeks. You know, it’s been like six weeks since I enjoyed myself and now, I think it was the right time to come back. I felt strong and, you know, this weekend I really took it step by step. It’s a track you can end up in the wall really quickly. I didn’t need that to gain the confidence, so it was a very slow build-up, but it brought me here. So, I’m very, very happy for an actual first proper podium on pure pace. So I’m very, very delighted.      Q: And that tells you as well, like, the wrist is okay after doing a whole race distance. This is something different. Must be happy now to continue the rest of the season?    IH:  Yeah, now I’m completely satisfied. Even though it’s a bit numb, I’m happy. So, yeah, I’m really looking forward to get racing. It’s going to be a very packed schedule, so, yeah, I can’t wait to be in Sepang.      Q: Good. Thanks, Isack. George, coming back quickly again, you closed the gap by 15 points here. It’s going to be intense weeks ahead. What is the game plan of George Russell now in that championship?    GR:  Win every race. I mean, that’s the game plan. You know, my team-mate’s had an incredible season. He’s been pretty flawless throughout, but now we’re getting to crunch time. But I’m just going to focus on myself. You know, if I continue delivering performances like I’ve done this weekend, no matter what happens towards the end of the season, I’ll be happy because it’s been a real tough period for me but I feel like I’ve come through the other side.      PRESS CONFERENCE        Q: George, what a weekend for you. Pole position yesterday by eight tenths, then victory today by one tenth. But just tell us what it all means to you.    GR:  Yeah, it feels great, to be honest. I’m very proud of the resilience that I and my close group of engineers have shown during the tough periods this year because there’s been a lot of hard work to overcome some of the challenges, to adapt my driving style to suit this new car better. And F1 is so tough, you don’t get opportunities to practice this, and finally it’s coming to me a bit more intuitively than it once did, and I’m gaining confidence. And especially on circuits like this, it just allows you to eke out that little bit more on the brakes, get that little bit closer to the walls, and it’s been a flawless weekend.      Q: You’re gaining confidence. Do you feel rejuvenated?    GR:  I think I never lost that faith in myself, even through a tough moments I knew there was a reason why I was off the pace. It wasn’t like I just suddenly forgot how to drive, and I knew I would be able to find it again. I just had to be patient. So, I feel confident. You know, it’s been four races since the break. I’ve been on the front row in three of them, three podiums from the four races. I feel I can fight for victory week-in, week-out now.      Q: Let’s break down the race. It was definitely one of two halves. You looked serene out front in the first stint. Were you happier on the Medium tyre?    GR:  Well, I think Max and myself were probably the two quickest drivers out there, and the soft tyre looked the best tyre, so I think that was maybe not allowing Max to get past Piastri. But, yeah, clearly that final stint, the two of us were exceptionally fast and, you know, we were pulling a second a lap almost to the rest of the field, which was really good fun, to be honest. It felt like qualifying laps, one after another, and I knew I couldn’t make a single mistake. But certainly, the last 10 laps were a bit more tense than the first 40.      Q: Talk us through the Safety Car restarts. Did they play out as you’d hoped?    GR:  Yeah, I mean, it’s the first restart I’ve done this season from the lead. These power units are very challenging at restarts, getting the battery in the right place for turbo spinning at the right speed, and I always do good preparation on what I want to do at a restart. It needs a lot more thought into it than ever before. But, you know, I was keeping an eye on my mirrors where Max was, and I had waited for that moment when the gap was just slightly larger and managed to break him because I knew if he saw half a chance, he would have been sending it down the inside. So, I was pleased with it.      Q: You’re happy with the car here, you’re happy with your performance. Are you confident that it’ll be the same next weekend at a permanent racetrack like Sepang?    GR:  I’m really excited. We’ve got the upgrades coming soon. That’s going to be a good step forward. Our car has been working exceptionally well on the low-drag circuits. We’ve got a really efficient car, so here at Monza we’ve been exceptionally fast. But I think from next week onwards, we’re hoping to make a bigger step to the rest of the field. But nothing’s sure until we see how it pans out in reality.      Q: Alright, very well done. Thank you very much for that, George. Max, let’s come to you. Great race by you, very well done. Given how close you were at the line, does today feel like a “what if” race for you? What if you’d started a little bit higher up the grid?    MV:  Yeah, I mean, we should have done that, right? I mean, that’s what happened yesterday. You know, you have a problem and then that means that you have to start P8. But I think even if I started second, I think the pace of George, it would have been very hard to pass. So maybe I could have followed him a bit better, of course, then in that first stint. Then you box, you’re second, behind, and then probably we would have done the same race, just pushing each other along. It would have for sure made my first stint a bit easier instead of overtaking all the cars that I had to. But, yeah, for sure the Soft tyre was much better than the Medium because I just had the first few laps in the first stint were very strong, but then, yeah, the tyres were just not working and it was quite a bit of, like, just surviving in the first stint, trying to go as long as possible. And then the Safety Car actually came at the right time to swap to the Soft tyres. And then I have to say that, yeah, those last laps were very enjoyable because there was barely any deg, really. We were just pushing to the end and the gap was always, like, one second, 1.1, so that was nice. And, of course, it looked close on the line, but I think that was more because I think George suffered from a little bit of boost lag in 15 with the yellow flag. So if you look at the last stint, it was always one second, so that’s probably also where we would have finished.      Q: How much of a boost is the performance of the car here with the upgrades, both for you and the whole team?    MV:  Yeah, it was good. I mean, the car was feeling very good all weekend. Okay, then we had the issue in qualifying with the engine. We still, of course, have some limitations with the car that I’ve mentioned many times that probably are not fixable for this year. So we know that for next year that needs a lot of work. But the balance in the car was strong. But like George said, for Malaysia, if they’re bringing an upgrade, it’s going to look a little bit more difficult for us.      Q: This was podium number seven for you this year. Are there any tracks that you’re particularly looking forward to coming up where you think you can be this competitive again?    MV:  We don’t know. I mean, if Mercedes is bringing an upgrade and it works, then they take a step ahead, and that’s not what you want. It will make it even more difficult to win, but we’ll try every single weekend and, of course, if the opportunity is there, we go for it.      Q: Max, very well done to you. Thank you for that. Isack, let’s come to you. What a comeback. Your second podium of the season after six weeks out. Just how sweet does this moment feel for you?    IH:  Yeah, I must say I came back at the right time in terms of an injury point of view and, at the same time, in terms of what the car is capable of. You know, the way I left the car in Budapest, I was not really satisfied, and coming back after a couple of races, definitely made a step. So, yeah, definitely happy about that. And, you know, in terms of the approach, I took it really slowly, the whole weekend, because it’s a demanding track to come back to. I don’t want to be in the wall. And, yeah, like I said, it’s a tough track to come back to. The approach was great. It brought me to that P3. So, yeah, I can’t really do much better than that.      Q: As you say, it’s a tough track. Any issues at all with the wrist?    IH:  No.      Q: And then when you look at the weekend as a whole, just how much have you missed racing over these last six weeks?    IH:  Yeah, it’s been a moment now. I felt like I had, like, a whole winter break, which is not really what you want in the middle of the season. So, yeah, I definitely missed it. You know, the adrenaline, those Q3 laps, the restart, and, yeah, it’s good to be back fighting with the other drivers. It’s what I love to do. So hopefully I use a bit more my brain when I go boxing next time.      Q: There was some radio chat about vibrations in the gearbox while you were behind the Safety Car. Did that clear up once the race went green?    IH:  No, it was quite noisy and I felt a lot of vibrations. I was a bit stressed, to be honest. I wasn’t really sure, but everything was fine until the very end. But, yeah, let’s see if it’s just some irrelevant noise or actually relevant. Let’s see.      Q: Okay. Look, final one. Just how much confidence does this weekend as a whole give you going to Sepang next weekend?    IH:  Yeah, a lot. You know, in the end, the Monaco podium, of course it was a podium, but it was not on pure pace, not because I qualified in the top three or whatever. You know, I felt like this is my first time with the team that I actually get to do a very clean weekend and actually, like, fight my way into that podium. So actually, for me, it feels like a real first and, yeah, it gives me good confidence heading into the next races.     QUESTIONS FROM THE FLOOR      Q: (Frédéric Ferret – L’Equipe) Question to George Russell. What does the Grand Slam mean for you? Question for Max: what does the podium of Isack mean for the team and how do you rate him? And question for Isack: you have the Zandvoort trophy on your helmet. Do you plan to make the same helmet next week?    GR:  Yeah, I think it’s probably my first Grand Slam in Formula 1 and, for sure, the most dominant weekend I’ve had in my career. So that has come at a really great moment. And also to achieve it on a circuit that requires so much commitment and confidence, I’m really proud of because I think it would have been very easy for me to lose the faith this season. Not necessarily about winning the championship, but in terms of my ability, and that never happened.   MV:  Yeah, well, this is what the team wants, to have the two cars on the podium when possible. So, maximising the result, and I think we did that today. So that’s very good. And, yeah, for sure, I mean, it’s working really well with Isack in the team and we just need to keep that going.      Q: How do you rate him, just to follow up?    MV:  Yeah, like, it’s working really well within the team, you know. So, of course, I mean, if you’re on the podium together, then I think you’re doing a good job.   IH:  I mean, it was pure coincidence. I should have raced that helmet in Zandvoort. I made it, so I wanted to, even though I skipped those races, wear it for that occasion. But now it’s a retired helmet and has a podium, so it’s good.      Q: (Leonid Kliuev – GrandePremio.com) Question for all three. Behind you, Franco was out of control into Turn 1 at the restart. Several people were taken out. Franco apologised. Lando said that, and I’m paraphrasing, he didn’t see the replay, but whoever is taking people out in this fashion should have a race ban, and he emphasised the race ban. Is that perhaps too harsh for your liking?     GR:  Yeah, I think that’s too harsh, personally. I think Safety Car restarts, cold tyres, a very small mistake can have big consequences. And from what I saw today, that’s what it looked like. It was a small error that had a big consequence. I think, personally, race bans should come from drivers intentionally doing something very dangerous and very reckless. So I think it was unfortunate.   MV:  Yeah, I think as long, of course, the driver that caused it is aware of what he did, right, and apologised. And, I mean, yeah, that happens. I mean, like, a small mistake or misjudgement, you lock up, it’s on the inside, low grip, and, of course, then I guess a bit unfortunate that it involves so many cars. But, yeah, unfortunate, happens, and it’s not nice, I think. Not nice for anyone involved, right? But like George said, I think, yeah, a race ban probably is a bit much.   IH:  From   my side, I think the track is not good enough. You move out of the racing line, it starts to be very bumpy. It’s hard to generate temperature behind the Safety Car, it’s going quite slowly. So then, yeah, you just overdo it and then it has big, big consequences. So, I think, yeah, a race ban is way too harsh.      Q: (Ronald Vording – Motorsport.com) It’s a question to both Red Bull drivers. Has your feeling behind the wheel, the feeling in the car, changed at all with this upgrade? So, do you feel more confident to attack the corners now, or is it simply quicker but still with the same issues?    IH:  Yeah, to be honest, Baku is a very specific track, specific tarmac. But like I said, to me, the way the car was behaving in terms of through-corner balance this weekend, from lap one in FP1, I was like, “Okay, this is looking pretty good.” Then the second half of the car, we’re lacking compared to Mercedes, definitely. But, you know, in terms of handling on the brakes, the car was, to me, compared to Budapest, it definitely did a step. So, yeah, I’m really pleased with that.   MV:  Yeah, I mean, it’s a unique track. It’s, like, mainly 90-degree corners. But, yeah, it felt probably a little bit more together balance-wise. But like I said, we have other issues in the car that we really need to fix because there is also just free lap time in that, and that’s what we are working on. But the performance items, they worked well and we’ve been fairly happy all weekend, really, with what I had from the car.      Q: (Phil Duncan – PA) George, after the race you spoke about your plan now is to go and win every race. It’s the crunch part of the season. You obviously don’t have the target on your back that Kimi does. Do you think that you can use that to your advantage, that you’re chasing and that you can help apply the pressure that way?    GR:  Yeah, for sure. There’s much less pressure on me than there is him. As I said yesterday, he’s had an incredibly flawless season. Yesterday was probably his first mistake of this whole season in a proper session, qualifying, race, and he still came home in P5 today. I didn’t really consider myself in this fight for a number of races, purely because my performance wasn’t strong enough. Now I feel like if the season were to have started today, or since the summer break, you know, I feel very much I would have been able to fight. Now I’ve got this big deficit. It can change quick. So I’m not chasing that. I’m chasing to win every race, and what will be, will be.      Q: (Sergey Podosenov – News.ru) As we have seen today, Baku City Circuit proved its unpredictable nature. How did the unique challenges of racing in Azerbaijan today impact your strategy and mindset on the way to the podium? Thank you.     GR:  Yeah, well, I must say Max and I spoke about this. The final stint, I think, is the most amount of fun I’ve had in a race for as long as I can remember because the tyre felt great. We were pushing flat out every single lap. It was like qualifying one after another. You needed to be so alert around this circuit because the walls are so close, especially through the castle. You’re threading the needle. But, yeah, those final 10 laps felt really, really fun. And it almost felt like the stories I hear of the drivers in the early-mid 2000s, of when every lap was like a qualifying lap. The heart rate is higher, you’re pushing the limit every single lap, there’s no management. We’ve had a lot of conversations this year about PU energy management, but the tyre management is still there and it has been there for years and years. But just with how the temperatures and the circuit fell out today, with the tyres there was no management, and that was exceptionally fun.   MV:  Yeah, exactly that. I mean, last stint was fun. Kissed a few walls as well, just to leave my mark here in Baku. So, yeah, it’s always very challenging around here, qualifying and in the race now at the end as well, just pushing flat out. Comes, of course, with risk, being close to certain walls on the inside, the outside. But it’s cool.      ENDS     FIA Formula One World Championship    Formula 1   SEASON 2026  Sport  Circuit 1SportFIA Formula One World ChampionshipCircuitSEASON 2026Formula 100 Saturday, September 26, 2026 - 6:47pm  Saturday, September 26, 2026 - 6:47pm

title: WEC: Alpine on pole at Fuji after rain leads to qualifying cancellation
summary: Sport news Heavy rain swept across Fuji Speedway ahead of the scheduled start of the LMGT3 qualifying session, which began on time but was red-flagged after François Heriau went off in his #21 VISTA AF Corse Ferrari.  The decision was then taken to cancel the remaining qualifying sessions due to the forecast of heavier rain and fog at Fuji Speedway.  That meant that, in accordance with the regulations, the grid was set according to the best times from the three Free Practice sessions held across Friday and Saturday morning.  Victor Martins’ FP2 time of 1m40.594s ensured that the #36 Alpine will start from pole position, marking the first-ever WEC pole for the A424 Hypercar.  It was a double celebration for the French manufacturer as the #35 car will join its sister Hypercar on the front row, putting Alpine in a strong position to defend last year’s victory at the venue.  Second on the grid should initially have been the #007 Aston Martin Valkyrie, but it was demoted to fourth after receiving a penalty for causing a collision in the morning’s FP3 session.  Starting third on the grid will be the #17 Genesis Magma Hypercar, meaning the Korean manufacturer will begin tomorrow’s race from by far its best-ever starting position.  In the LMGT3 category, the #77 Proton Competition Ford Mustang will start from pole position after setting the fastest FP2 time on Friday afternoon. It marks the first pole position for a Ford Mustang since the Lone Star Le Mans race at COTA in September 2025.       WEC  Endurance  6 Hours of Fuji  WEC   Sport 1SportWECWECEndurance6 Hours of Fuji00 Saturday, September 26, 2026 - 9:08am  Saturday, September 26, 2026 - 9:08am

title: FIA President Mohammed Ben Sulayem Meets Lebanese President Joseph Aoun to Discuss Shared Motorsport Priorities
summary: FIA news Mohammed Ben Sulayem, President of the FIA, met with Lebanese President His Excellency Joseph Aoun today after attending the Rally of Lebanon, an event he won four times in a distinguished rally driving career which established him as a sporting ambassador for the Arab world.  The meeting at Baabda Palace provided an opportunity to reflect on the continued success of the event, and Lebanon’s position as a rallying stronghold in the Middle East.  Ben Sulayem accepted an official invitation from the Automobile and Touring Club of Lebanon and President Nabil ‘Billy’ Karam to attend the 48th Rally of Lebanon. The fourth round of this year’s FIA Middle East Rally Championship reached its finish at the ATCL in Kaslik, Jounieh last night (Sunday) with victory going to Lebanon’s Roger Feghali and co-driver Joseph Matar.   “I was pleased to meet with President Aoun and discuss our shared priorities for the future of motorsport,”   said FIA President Ben Sulayem.   “The Rally of Lebanon provided me with many great memories during my rally driving career, and I’m thrilled to once again experience the excitement this event creates for competitors and the country’s passionate motor sport fans.”    “The event has a rich history embedded in the origins of Middle East motorsport. It is firmly established as the home for asphalt rallying in the region, and plays a key role in our plans to ensure the long-term future of the FIA Middle East Rally Championship.    “Lebanon has always felt like a special place for me, and I want to thank the ATCL and its President, Nabil Karam, for their warm welcome and hospitality. I’m delighted to have met up again with some of the friends I have made at the club, and across the country over the years.”   Ben Sulayem’s legendary rally-driving achievements brought him widespread recognition, and he was awarded the President’s Cup by Lebanese President Amine Gemayel in 1987, and the Medal of Honour from Lebanese President Emile Lahoud in 1999.  Each of his four victories in the Rally of Lebanon, in 1987, 1991, 1998 and 1999, helped him secure the FIA Middle East Rally Championship title, which he won 14 times overall. He achieved the last three of those victories alongside his long-time co-driver Ronan Morgan.  Beyond his success in Middle East rallying, Ben Sulayem recorded his first overseas win in Turkey in 1991, and secured World Rally Championship Group N victories in Spain and Argentina over the following two years. He retired from competitive rallying in 2002.  In July, the FIA announced a landmark long-term commercial rights agreement for the FIA WRC and FIA European Rally Championship, following the acquisition of WRC Promoter GmbH by Cosmobilis and Park Square Capital. Designed to bring significant new investment into the sport, the biggest deal in the history of these championships supported the FIA’s vision under President Ben Sulayem, who said at the time:  “Rallying is a huge part of my personal story. It has shaped who I am and how I work, and I am deeply committed to its future.”       ENDS    About the FIA   The Fédération Internationale de l'Automobile (FIA) is the governing body for world motor sport and the federation for mobility organisations globally. It is a non-profit organisation committed to driving innovation and championing safety, sustainability and equality across motor sport and mobility.  Founded in 1904, with offices in Paris, London and Geneva, the FIA brings together 246 Member Organisations across five continents, representing millions of road users, motor sport professionals and volunteers. It develops and enforces regulations for motor sport, including seven FIA World Championships, to ensure worldwide competitions are safe and fair for all.
